summary.text: The front matter of WHO's Global hepatitis report 2026, with the cover, ISBN and copyright page, licence terms and suggested citation. The table of contents lists chapters on global commitments and targets, epidemic status and trends, prevention, diagnosis and treatment, and the road to elimination, plus annexes on methods, reporting and Health Assembly resolutions. Short statements from the WHO Director-General and the Director of the Department for HIV, Tuberculosis, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Infections say progress is real but too slow and uneven to reach the 2030 elimination targets and call for faster, integrated action.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Viral hepatitis is one of the world’s most important public 
health challenges. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis 
C virus (HCV) continue to cause chronic infection in hundreds of millions of people, leading to cirrhosis, liver cancer and over 1 million premature deaths each year, even 
though both infections are preventable and treatable. 
Together, HBV and HCV account for over 95% of global 
mortality caused by viral hepatitis, with hepatitis A virus 
(HAV), hepatitis D virus (HDV) and hepatitis E virus (HEV) 
accounting for the remainder.

summary.text: The introduction to the Global hepatitis report 2026 explains that hepatitis B and C cause chronic infection in hundreds of millions of people and over 95% of viral hepatitis deaths, and outlines how the five hepatitis viruses are transmitted. It recalls the commitment of all Member States to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030 and the five interventions that can achieve it, from hepatitis B vaccination to testing and treatment, alongside research on a hepatitis B cure and a hepatitis C vaccine. It describes the report as the fourth global assessment since reporting began in 2016, covering 2015–2024 and drawing on data from 140 reporting Member States and model-based estimates, and sets out the chapter structure. Box 1.1 gives basic facts on each hepatitis virus, and the section ends with an overview of the latest status against the 2030 impact and service coverage targets.

summary.text: Traces how viral hepatitis rose onto the global health agenda, from a 1975 Health Assembly resolution on blood safety and the 1992 call to add hepatitis B vaccine to infant schedules, through the 2010 and 2014 resolutions, World Hepatitis Day, the Global Hepatitis Programme and the 2015 SDG target 3.3. It describes WHO's first Global health sector strategy on viral hepatitis (2016–2021), which set the goal of elimination by 2030 with a 90% cut in new infections and a 65% cut in deaths from 2015 levels, five intervention areas, a two-phase expansion and a diagnosis and treatment cascade. The section ends with a table of the current 2030 impact and service coverage targets and the latest status of progress against them.

blocks.title: Epidemic status and trends
blocks.content:
There are five hepatitis viruses: A, B, C, D and E (HAV, 
HBV, HCV, HDV and HEV). This chapter focuses on HBV 
and HCV, because they account for more than 95% of viral 
hepatitis-related deaths (Chapter  1) and are the forms 
of hepatitis for which global targets have been set in the 
World Health Organization (WHO) Global health sector 
strategy on viral hepatitis, 2022–2030 (GHSS 2022–2030) 
(Chapter 2). 
People can be infected with HBV and HCV through 
exposure to infected blood (HBV and HCV) or other bodily 
fluids (HBV). In highly endemic areas, most chronic HBV 
infections occur in child

summary.text: Opens the chapter on the status and trends of the viral hepatitis epidemic, which concentrates on hepatitis B and C because they cause over 95% of hepatitis deaths, explaining how each virus is transmitted, how infection progresses silently over decades to cirrhosis and liver cancer, and how incidence, prevalence and mortality are defined. Reviews the available interventions (hepatitis B vaccination, antiviral treatment and prophylaxis, a 12-week direct-acting antiviral cure for hepatitis C, blood safety, infection control and harm reduction) and the 2030 elimination targets. Its key findings put 2024 deaths at about 1.1 million from HBV and 240 000 from HCV, with HBV deaths up 17% since 2015 and concentrated in the African and Western Pacific regions, HCV deaths down 12%, and an estimated 240 million people living with chronic HBV and 47 million with HCV infection. Closes with a section on hepatitis D, which weighs most on low- and middle-income countries with limited testing, and a table comparing the latest coverage indicators with their 2030 targets.

blocks.title: Prevention, diagnosis and treatment
blocks.content:
Viral hepatitis remains a leading global health problem 
(Chapter 3). 
Globally in 2024, the sequelae of chronic hepatitis B 
virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections – liver 
cirrhosis and hepatocellular cancer (HCC) – caused a combined total of 1.3 million deaths (95% uncertainty interval [UI]: 1.1–1.7 million). This included 1.1 million (95% UI: 
0.9–1.3 million) HBV-related deaths and 240 000 (95% UI: 
160 000–370 000) HCV-related deaths. 
Globally in 2024, there were an estimated 240 million 
people living with a chronic HBV infection (95% UI: 202–

summary.text: Presents the latest coverage data for hepatitis prevention, diagnosis and treatment, recalling that HBV and HCV caused 1.3 million deaths and 1.8 million new infections in 2024 and setting out the coverage levels the global health sector strategy requires by 2025 and 2030. Covers the most impactful interventions first: hepatitis B birth-dose and infant vaccination (with 118 of 194 Member States providing universal birth-dose vaccination as of December 2025), antiviral prophylaxis against mother-to-child transmission, and antiviral treatment for chronic HBV and HCV infection. Later sections address blood and injection safety in health care and harm-reduction services for people who inject drugs, who account for about 44% of new HCV infections. Concludes that harm-reduction coverage is far below recommended levels, with about 35 needles and syringes distributed per person who injects drugs each year against a 2030 target of 300, only 18 in 100 having access to OAMT, and only five countries reaching high coverage of both services.

blocks.title: The road to elimination
blocks.content:
The possibility that viral hepatitis could be eliminated 
as a public health threat worldwide was first recognized 
by all Member States of the World Health Organization 
(WHO) in 2014 (Chapter 2). Subsequently, the goal of the 
first WHO global health sector strategy on viral hepatitis (GHSS 2016–2021) (4), adopted by all Member States 
in 2016, was defined as elimination of viral hepatitis as a 
public health threat by 2030. This goal was retained in the 
second GHSS, for 2022–2030 (3).
The 2030 elimination targets are: 
	
f a 95% reduction in the annual number of new hepatitis 
B virus (HBV

summary.text: Traces the goal of eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030 from its recognition by WHO Member States in 2014 through the two global health sector strategies, and notes that the targets can be met with existing vaccines and antivirals whose prices have fallen sharply since 2015. Finds progress between 2015 and 2024 too slow: new HBV infections fell by 32% and new HCV infections by 8.1%, HBV-related deaths rose by 17% while HCV-related deaths fell by 12%, and in 2024 birth-dose coverage was 45%, under 5% of people with HBV were on treatment and HCV treatment coverage was 20%. Sets out five priorities for global and regional action: scaling up HBV treatment, especially in the African and Western Pacific regions, and HCV treatment, especially in the Eastern Mediterranean Region; raising birth-dose vaccination and antiviral prophylaxis coverage, especially in Africa; and making nonmedical injections safer through harm reduction. Gives 10 country examples, ending with Thailand's free nationwide HCV test-and-treat campaign, which in three years reached 7.3 million people, found almost 75 000 infections and treated more than 50 000.

blocks.title: Methodological notes
blocks.content:
This annex summarizes the main updates to methods 
used to produce epidemiological estimates (incidence, 
prevalence and mortality) and associated estimates of 
diagnostic and treatment coverage, compared with those 
used in previous World Health Organization (WHO) global 
reports on hepatitis, published in 2017 and 2024 (1, 2). The 
updates reflect the availability of new data, refinements 
in modelling methods and enhanced calibration procedures that, overall, improve the accuracy, comparability 
and interpretability of global and regional trends. 
The annex also highlights specific methodol

summary.text: Summarizes how the methods behind the report's estimates of hepatitis incidence, prevalence, mortality and diagnosis and treatment coverage have changed since the 2017 and 2024 reports, chiefly a full recalibration of the HBV and HCV models with the Center for Disease Analysis Foundation that revises past figures, so earlier estimates should not be compared with these. Notes, for example, that HBV prevalence among children under five in 2020 is now put at 0.65% rather than 0.9%, that the 2015 baseline of 6–10 million new infections has been revised downwards, and that time series for 2015–2024 are now provided. Explains that country maps and target assessments rely on modelled estimates, which should prompt national review rather than serve as official proof of elimination, describes how the HBV and HCV cascades of care are presented, and announces updated online country profiles.

summary.text: Describes WHO's global hepatitis reporting, held every two years, which in 2025 gathered data for 2024 on the hepatitis B and C burden and on intervention coverage, plus the status of national policies, between July and December. Outlines its phases: a data collection form in four languages, nominated national focal points with access to an online platform launched on 25 June 2025 and backed by webinars, a priority order of validated country data, regionally validated data and WHO estimates, validation support, and a country review of the final datasets in November. A table shows that 140 of the 194 Member States reported data, with participation varying by WHO region.

summary.text: Summarizes the two World Health Assembly resolutions on viral hepatitis, WHA63.18 of 2010 and WHA67.6 of 2014, listing what each committed Member States to and asked of WHO. The 2010 resolution designated 28 July as World Hepatitis Day and called for better surveillance, integrated prevention and care, protection of health workers, access to medicines including through TRIPS flexibilities, and WHO support on goals, research, burden estimates and resource mobilization. The 2014 resolution called on Member States for national multisectoral strategies, stronger immunization including a timely hepatitis B birth dose, civil society involvement, surveillance, blood and organ safety, food and water safety, and infection control.
